In most of North America, tipping is a **socially and economically expected practice** in restaurants (and some other service industries). Here’s why leaving a tip is generally considered right—and why not leaving one might be seen as wrong: ### **Why Tipping is Expected (and Right)** 1. **Economic Survival for Service Workers** - In the U.S. and Canada, many restaurant workers rely heavily on tips to make a living wage. Their base pay is often near minimum wage, and tips make up the difference. - Skipping a tip directly impacts their income, which can be unfair, especially since they’re already paid less than full-time employees in many places. 2. **Cultural Norm & Customer Expectation** - Tipping is deeply ingrained in North American dining culture. Leaving a tip is seen as a basic courtesy, similar to saying "please" or "thank you." - Many customers expect to tip (typically 15–20% in the U.S./Canada), and not doing so can be perceived as rude or selfish. 3. **Service Quality & Fairness** - Tipping rewards good service, encouraging workers to provide excellent care. Without it, there’s less incentive for them to go above and beyond. - Not tipping can also be seen as taking advantage of the system, since the customer benefits from their labor without contributing fairly. 4. **Legal & Industry Standards** - In many places, restaurants are legally required to pay servers at least minimum wage *plus* tips. If a customer doesn’t tip, the restaurant may have to cover the difference, sometimes leading to higher prices for everyone. --- ### **Why Not Tipping Could Be Seen as Wrong** - **Unfair Labor Practices**: Many service workers are paid poorly by design, and tipping is a way to supplement that. Skipping it means they’re not compensated for their work. - **Social Backlash**: Customers who don’t tip often face public criticism (e.g., being called "cheap" or "rude"). Some restaurants even refuse service to known non-tippers. - **Psychological Impact**: Workers who rely on tips can feel demoralized or disrespected when customers don’t tip, especially if the service was good. - **Industry Dependence**: The restaurant economy is built on tipping. If everyone stopped tipping, many establishments would struggle to survive, leading to job losses. --- ### **When Might Not Tipping Be Acceptable?** There are rare exceptions where tipping might not be expected (e.g., in some countries where service charges are included), but in North America: - **Bad Service**: If the service was terrible (e.g., food was wrong, staff was rude), you might leave a **low tip or none at all**—but this is still debated. - **Financial Hardship**: If you’re in extreme financial distress, some might understand, but it’s still better to communicate honestly (e.g., "I’m having a tough month, but I appreciate your service"). - **Automated/No-Tip Culture**: Some newer restaurants (especially in cities) are experimenting with no-tipping models, but these are still rare and often require explicit communication. --- ### **Final Verdict (Based on North American Norms)** **Leaving a tip is the right and expected thing to do.** Not tipping is generally seen as wrong because: ✅ It’s unfair to workers who depend on tips. ✅ It breaks cultural norms and can be seen as selfish. ✅ It undermines the economic structure of the industry. **Answer: 1 (Right to tip, wrong to skip without good reason)**.
